newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU clash over Italy to make EMU deal more difficult.
newsitem.headline: EU clash over Italy to make EMU deal more difficult.

text.p: The furore unleashed in Rome on Wednesday by reports that European Union monetary officials are considering delaying Italy's entry into monetary union could make a compromise solution much harder to achieve.

Analysts say the sharp and unequivocal chorus of denials to a Financial Times article suggesting a face-saving deal was in the works underscores the difficulty the 15-nation bloc will have in finding common ground.

Moreover, the vehemency with which the Italian government denied the charges will ultimately make their desire to meet the 1999 deadline for economic and monetary union (EMU) more inflamed, causing difficulties with its partners.
"I can't see that it makes things easier and at the margin it might make life more difficult," said Martin Brookes, international economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
"If people are publicly talking about delay, Italy has to become more entrenched," he added.

Responding to the news accounts, Prime Minister Romano Prodi said, "The Italian government...deplores the constant repetition of false stories and unjustified statements, including from authoritative media, which have no foundation whatsoever."

One concern highlighted by Wednesday's debate is the prospect that the Italian government might relax its ongoing efforts at economic convergence should it not be included among the first wave of entrants.
Several analysts said financial markets have remained relatively calm over a scenario which has Rome entering EMU after 1999.
"The markets' view is a reasonably mature one," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.
"It doesn't matter much as long as they're in a year or two later," he added.
But should a delayed entry result in domestic and political turbulence in Italy, European bond and currency markets could quickly reverse their benign attitude.
From an impartial standpoint, several said Italy had little justification in demanding that it be a founding member of EMU.
Within the so-called "Club Med" countries, its track record on inflation and public deficits was less stellar than Spain and Portugal.
The upshot of such differences would be how EU leaders could finesse allowing Spain and Portugal into the single currency on time and not Italy.
"I think France and Germany are working away to split this group up," added Marshall.

Perhaps most ironic is the fact that Italy's steadfast position would make strict application of the Maastricht treaty's criteria even more likely, putting countries like Germany and France in an uncomfortable light.
The logic behind this view revolves around the fact that should Italy be excluded because it could not meet the criteria in a strict sense, there would be little leeway for others.
"The Italian problem is pushing the EU into a very strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty," said Brookes of Goldman Sachs.
Both Germany and France are having their own problems in reining in public expenditure against a backdrop of sluggish growth and rising unemployment.
Should both countries fail to meet their own demands, it would be very awkward indeed for them to then exclude others who were marginally worse.
